subject: Architecture
title: The Mile-High Debate: Should We Keep Going?
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Mile-High Debate: Should We Keep Going?.

hook.text: Frank Lloyd Wright proposed a mile-high tower in 1956. Today, engineers say it's possible. But should we?

buildup.text: A mile-high building would hold 100,000 people. Evacuating them in an emergency could take eight hours.

discovery.text: Above 2,000 feet, buildings create their own weather — fog, ice, and pressure changes affect occupants.

twist.text: Studies show people above the 40th floor report higher anxiety and lower wellbeing than lower-floor residents.

climax.text: Some architects argue we should build wider and greener, not taller — dense low-rises use land better.

punchline.text: We can build a mile high. The real question is whether anyone should live there.

quiz.question: What problem occurs in buildings above 2,000 feet tall?
options: Cell phone signals cannot reach that height
The buildings create their own weather including fog and ice
Construction cranes cannot lift materials that high

details.summary: Frank Lloyd Wright proposed a mile-high (1,609-meter) skyscraper in 1956. While engineering could theoretically achieve this, critics question whether ever-taller buildings serve human needs or merely satisfy ego. The debate balances engineering ambition against environmental impact and livability.
details.whyItMatters: The mile-high question forces architecture to confront its own limits — not structural but ethical. Should we build to the maximum possible height, or is there an optimal human scale that taller is not better than?
takeaways: Frank Lloyd Wright proposed a mile-high tower in 1956
Engineering could likely achieve the height; purpose is debated
Critics question whether extreme height serves human needs

faq.question: Could a mile-high building actually be built today?
faq.answer: Most structural engineers say the engineering is theoretically achievable with current materials and knowledge. The barriers are financial (cost would be enormous), practical (elevator travel is 15+ minutes), and philosophical (whether anyone would want to live or work there).

faq.question: What was Wright's mile-high design?
faq.answer: Called The Illinois, Wright's 1956 proposal was a tapering tripod tower with atomic-powered elevators and parking for 15,000 cars. It was visionary but impractical for its era. The design influenced later supertall concepts and kept the idea of extreme height alive in architectural discourse.
